Title: Diagnosis

Details: The failing test case `testUnsafeDeSerialization` in `MultiValueMapTest` is designed to cover deserialization safety. It tries to deserialize a `MultiValueMap` using a collection class of `String.class` which is not a valid collection class (String does not implement `Collection`), expecting this unsafe class to be rejected. The test expects an `UnsupportedOperationException` to be thrown during deserialization.

Looking at the `deserialize` method used in the test, it straightforwardly reads the object from an `ObjectInputStream` with `iis.readObject()` without any safety checks or filtering against unsafe classes.

The `multiValueMap` factory method accepts a `Map` and a `Class<C>` representing a collection class, instantiating a new `MultiValueMap` with a custom `ReflectionFactory`. This factory creates new instances of the provided collection type by invoking `clazz.newInstance()` without checks, as seen in the `ReflectionFactory.create()` method.

The `MultiValueMap` uses this factory to create its collection values, but on deserialization, it reads the map field directly from the stream without re-validating or resetting the factory, as shown in the `readObject` method: it reads the underlying map but does not enforce any check on the collection class or the factory used for the collections.

This means that if a malicious serialized payload uses an unsafe class as the collection class for values (such as `String` or worse, classes that can cause arbitrary code execution when instantiated), the deserialization will not prevent this and will silently accept it.

Hence, the vulnerability described in the current bug report about arbitrary remote code execution is possible because the `MultiValueMap` deserialization mechanism does not enforce class safety or whitelist validations, allowing the injection of arbitrary classes during deserialization via the collection class factory.

The test correctly identifies this by trying to deserialize a map with `String.class` as the collection, expecting an error, but this exception is not thrown, leading to test failure.

Recent bug reports about deserialization problems related to other classes like `MultiKey` indicate that deserialization safety and readResolve methods were discussed elsewhere, further emphasizing that incorrect or missing safeguards on deserialization can cause security issues.

In summary, the root cause is that `MultiValueMap.readObject` does not perform any validation on the collection class or factory on deserialization, allowing unsafe classes and thus enabling arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities.

This matches the symptoms described in the current bug report and the failing test's expectations.

The fix should focus on adding safe deserialization checks or enforcing restrictions on collections classes during deserialization.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
